```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("presentation_setup.R")
```

**Purpose.** This notebook asks what the model's scores would mean for an actual
lending decision. It turns the final model's holdout predictions into default
rates by risk group, the effect of flagging the riskiest applicants, and a
comparison with a simple "no credit history, no loan" rule. It follows the success
definition in the business problem statement: a lower default rate at the same
approval rate, or a higher approval rate at the same default rate.

**Data and model.** Everything here uses the 61,502 holdout applicants the model
never saw in training, so nothing is in-sample. The model is a refit of the final
XGBoost model from `modeling.qmd` with the same hyperparameters, built by
`rebuild_presentation_cache.R`. Its holdout AUC is 0.7550, against 0.7556 in the
original run; the small gap comes from package-version differences.

**How to read the results.** Every policy below is a *retrospective* comparison on
historical applicants whose outcomes are already known. These are illustrations of
what the ranking could support, not measured results of a deployed policy. No
costs, revenue, or loan pricing are included.

```{r basics}
ho <- tibble(
  default    = as.integer(holdout_data$TARGET == 1),
  prob       = holdout_prob,
  credit     = holdout_data$AMT_CREDIT,
  has_bureau = holdout_data$has_bureau_record
)
n_ho      <- nrow(ho)
base_rate <- mean(ho$default)
per_10k   <- 10000 / n_ho

tibble(Item  = c("Holdout applicants", "Defaults", "Default rate", "Holdout AUC"),
       Value = c(num(n_ho), num(sum(ho$default)), pct(base_rate, 2),
                 sprintf("%.4f", check_auc))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## 1. Default rate by model risk decile

Applicants are ranked by predicted risk and split into ten equal groups
(deciles). If the model ranks well, the default rate should rise steadily from
decile 1 (safest) to decile 10 (riskiest).

```{r deciles}
ho <- ho |> mutate(decile = ntile(prob, 10))   # 10 = riskiest

deciles <- ho |>
  group_by(decile) |>
  summarise(applicants   = n(),
            avg_score    = mean(prob),
            default_rate = mean(default),
            defaults     = sum(default),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(decile)) |>
  mutate(share_of_defaults = defaults / sum(defaults),
         cumulative_share  = cumsum(share_of_defaults))

deciles |>
  mutate(across(c(avg_score, default_rate, share_of_defaults, cumulative_share),
                ~ pct(.x))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Holdout applicants by model risk decile (10 = riskiest)")

write_csv(deciles, file.path(results_dir, "deciles.csv"))
```

```{r decile-chart, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Default rate by model risk decile on the 61,502 holdout applicants. The safest and riskiest deciles are highlighted."}
decile_plot <- ggplot(deciles, aes(factor(decile), default_rate,
                                   fill = decile %in% c(1, 10))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(default_rate)), vjust = -0.4, size = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#CC0000", `FALSE` = "#A9B4D0"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "The riskiest tenth of applicants default far more than the safest",
       x = "Model risk decile (10 = riskiest)", y = "Default rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
decile_plot
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "decile_chart.png"), decile_plot, width = 11, height = 6, dpi = 200)
```

**Interpretation.** The default rate rises at every step, from
`r pct(deciles$default_rate[deciles$decile == 1])` in the safest decile to
`r pct(deciles$default_rate[deciles$decile == 10])` in the riskiest, and the riskiest
decile alone holds `r pct(deciles$share_of_defaults[deciles$decile == 10])` of all
defaults. A ranking this steep is what makes risk-based review possible: most of
the risk sits in a small, identifiable group.

## 2. Flagging the riskiest applicants

Each row below flags the riskiest 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% of holdout applicants and
shows what happens to the default rate among everyone else. "Flagged" could mean
declined, referred to an underwriter, or asked for more verification; the table
does not assume which.

```{r policies}
flag_policy <- function(q) {
  cutoff <- quantile(ho$prob, 1 - q)
  flag   <- ho$prob >= cutoff
  tibble(
    flagged_share         = mean(flag),
    defaults_caught       = sum(flag & ho$default == 1) / sum(ho$default),
    default_rate_flagged  = mean(ho$default[flag]),
    default_rate_approved = mean(ho$default[!flag]),
    relative_drop         = 1 - mean(ho$default[!flag]) / base_rate,
    good_borrowers_flagged = sum(flag & ho$default == 0) / sum(ho$default == 0),
    defaults_avoided_per_10k = sum(flag & ho$default == 1) * per_10k,
    defaulted_credit_avoided_per_10k = sum(ho$credit[flag & ho$default == 1]) * per_10k,
    score_cutoff          = cutoff
  )
}
policies <- map_dfr(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20), flag_policy)

policies |>
  mutate(across(c(flagged_share:good_borrowers_flagged), ~ pct(.x)),
         across(c(defaults_avoided_per_10k, defaulted_credit_avoided_per_10k), num),
         score_cutoff = round(score_cutoff, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Flagging the riskiest X% of applicants")

write_csv(policies, file.path(results_dir, "policies.csv"))
```

**Interpretation.** Flagging more applicants catches more defaults but also flags
more applicants who would have repaid (`good_borrowers_flagged`). Choosing where to
draw the line is a business decision that needs Home Credit's own costs and risk
appetite. This notebook shows the trade-off; it does not pick a cutoff.

## 3. Same approval rate: the model vs. "no credit history, no loan"

A traditional lender turns away anyone without a credit bureau record. This
compares that rule with the model turning away the same number of applicants,
namely the ones it rates riskiest.

**Which applicants count as "no credit history".** The rule here declines every
applicant with **no credit bureau record** (`has_bureau_record == 0`), which is
14.3% of the training data. This is a broader group than the `thin_file` feature in
`data_preparation.R`, which flags applicants with no bureau record *and* no credit
inquiry data. The `thin_file` feature is not used in this comparison.

**What kind of comparison this is.** It is retrospective: both policies are
applied to historical holdout applicants whose outcomes are already known. The
"no credit history, no loan" rule is a simplified benchmark, not Home Credit's
actual policy, and outcomes exist only for loans that were actually issued.

```{r rule-vs-model}
rule_decline  <- ho$has_bureau == 0
k             <- sum(rule_decline)
model_decline <- rank(-ho$prob, ties.method = "first") <= k

same_approval <- tibble(
  Policy = c("No credit history, no loan", "My model"),
  `Approval rate` = pct(c(1 - k / n_ho, 1 - k / n_ho)),
  `Default rate of approved loans` = pct(c(mean(ho$default[!rule_decline]),
                                           mean(ho$default[!model_decline])), 2),
  `Defaults per 10,000 applicants` = num(c(sum(ho$default[!rule_decline]),
                                           sum(ho$default[!model_decline])) * per_10k),
  `No-bureau-record applicants approved` = pct(c(0, mean(!model_decline[ho$has_bureau == 0])))
)
knitr::kable(same_approval)

# Same default rate as the rule: how many applicants can the model approve?
# Note: this cutoff is found by searching the holdout's own outcomes for the
# largest approval count that keeps the default rate at or below the rule's, so
# the result is optimistic (see the note after the tables).
rule_rate  <- mean(ho$default[!rule_decline])
safe_first <- ho$default[order(ho$prob)]
approve_n  <- max(which(cumsum(safe_first) / seq_len(n_ho) <= rule_rate))
same_default <- tibble(
  `Default rate held at` = pct(rule_rate, 2),
  `Rule approves`  = pct(1 - k / n_ho),
  `Model approves` = pct(approve_n / n_ho),
  `Extra approvals per 10,000 applicants` = num((approve_n - (n_ho - k)) * per_10k)
)
knitr::kable(same_default)

write_csv(same_approval, file.path(results_dir, "same_approval.csv"))
write_csv(same_default,  file.path(results_dir, "same_default.csv"))
```

**Interpretation.** At the same approval rate, the model-based policy approves
loans with a lower default rate than the rule, and it still approves most of the
applicants with no bureau record whom the rule turns away entirely. This is the
more defensible of the two comparisons: the model only has to choose *which*
applicants to decline, and the number declined is fixed by the rule.

**Caution on the same-default-rate comparison.** The second table should not be
used as a headline result. Its cutoff was chosen *using the holdout outcomes*, by
searching for the largest number of approvals that keeps the observed default rate
at or below the rule's. A cutoff tuned on the same data it is evaluated on
overstates how well it would hold up on new applicants.

## 4. Summary for the slides

```{r summary}
p10 <- policies |> filter(abs(flagged_share - 0.10) < 0.005)
fewer <- (sum(ho$default[!rule_decline]) - sum(ho$default[!model_decline])) * per_10k

summary_lines <- c(
  sprintf("# Business impact results (holdout, %s applicants)", num(n_ho)),
  "",
  sprintf("- Holdout AUC check: %.4f", check_auc),
  sprintf("- Riskiest decile default rate: %s; safest decile: %s",
          pct(deciles$default_rate[deciles$decile == 10]),
          pct(deciles$default_rate[deciles$decile == 1])),
  sprintf("- Flag riskiest 10%%: catches %s of defaults; approved default rate %s -> %s (%s lower)",
          pct(p10$defaults_caught), pct(base_rate, 2),
          pct(p10$default_rate_approved, 2), pct(p10$relative_drop)),
  sprintf("- Same approval rate as 'no credit history, no loan' (%s approved): default rate %s (rule) vs %s (model); %s fewer defaults per 10,000 applicants",
          pct(1 - k / n_ho), pct(rule_rate, 2),
          pct(mean(ho$default[!model_decline]), 2), num(fewer)),
  sprintf("- Applicants with no credit bureau record the model approves at that rate: %s",
          pct(mean(!model_decline[ho$has_bureau == 0]))),
  sprintf("- Same default rate as the rule (%s): model approves %s vs %s (%s more per 10,000 applicants); cutoff chosen using holdout outcomes, so optimistic",
          pct(rule_rate, 2), pct(approve_n / n_ho), pct(1 - k / n_ho),
          num((approve_n - (n_ho - k)) * per_10k)),
  "",
  "All comparisons are retrospective, on historical holdout applicants, with no costs included."
)
writeLines(summary_lines, file.path(results_dir, "business_impact_summary.md"))
cat(summary_lines, sep = "\n")
```

## 5. Limitations

- **Retrospective, not prospective.** Every policy is applied to historical applicants
  with known outcomes. A deployed policy would face new applicants and changing
  conditions.
- **Issued loans only.** Outcomes exist only for loans Home Credit actually issued, so
  this analysis cannot show how previously rejected applicants would have performed.
- **No costs.** Defaults avoided are counted, not valued. Lost revenue from declined
  good borrowers, loan sizes, and pricing are not modeled, so no financial savings
  are claimed.
- **Fairness not assessed.** Age and gender are among the model's influential
  predictors (see `modeling.qmd` and `02_personas.Rmd`). Any real policy would need a
  fairness and compliance review first.
- **Association, not causation.** The model ranks applicants by characteristics
  associated with default; it does not identify causes.
